title: Microcontrollers: boards, resets and quirks
summary: Which microcontroller board you have, what voltage its pins take, which USB chip and driver it needs, and how to force each family into its bootloader when uploads fail. It also covers the pins and power faults that stop boards booting, Chinese clone boards, reflashing ESP smart plugs and bulbs with Tasmota or ESPHome, and what to download now for programming with no internet.

steps.text: Find the board or chip in the first table and check its logic voltage before you wire anything to it.
steps.warn: Most of these boards are 3.3 V: 5 V on a pin can destroy them. MAINS CAN KILL: unplug a smart plug, bulb or other mains device before opening it, and never have it plugged in while a USB-serial adapter or computer is wired to it.

steps.text: Upload failing? Check the cable carries data, a port appears and its driver is installed, then force the bootloader with the reset table for your family.
Board resets, will not boot or behaves oddly? Check the quirks and clones tables for strapping pins, power and fake chips.
While you still have internet, download the tools, board packages and firmware in the last table.

notes:
Pin maps are in [Board pinouts](#ref/pinouts). Ready-made code is in [Microcontroller code templates](#ref/reference_mcu_code).

## Which board is it?

| Board (chip) | Logic | USB | Where it turns up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Uno R3 (ATmega328P), Mega 2560 (ATmega2560) | 5 V | ATmega16U2 on the board (Arduino Uno datasheet, Arduino Mega datasheet) | Kits, projects. Einsy RAMBo printer boards sold by Prusa use the ATmega2560 (Klipper Einsy) |
| Nano (ATmega328P) | 5 V | Official: FT232RL. Most clones: CH340 (Cow Pi Nano) | Kits. Melzi boards in the 2018 Ender-3 use the bigger ATmega1284P (Klipper Ender-3) |
| Leonardo, Pro Micro (ATmega32U4) | 5 V, 16 MHz; Pro Micro also 3.3 V, 8 MHz (SparkFun Pro Micro) | Built into the chip (Arduino Leonardo) | Kits |
| Pro Mini (ATmega328P) | 3.3 V, 8 MHz or 5 V, 16 MHz (SparkFun Pro Mini) | None: a USB-serial adapter on its 6-pin header (SparkFun Pro Mini) | Kits |
| ESP8266: NodeMCU, D1 mini, ESP-01 | 3.3 V (WEMOS D1 mini) | D1 mini: CH340 (WEMOS D1 mini). ESP-01: none | Wi-Fi smart plugs, bulbs, switches (Tasmota) |
| ESP32 (classic) | 3.3 V; 3.6 V absolute max (ESP32 datasheet) | DOIT DevKit V1: CP2102 (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting) | Smart plugs and switches (Tasmota); ESP32-CAM |
| ESP32-S2, S3, C3 | 3.3 V | Native USB: S2 and S3 serial and DFU, C3 serial only (Arduino-ESP32 USB). Some boards add a CP2102 (Heltec docs) | Smart devices (Tasmota), LoRa boards |
| Pico, Pico W (RP2040); Pico 2, 2 W (RP2350) | 3.3 V. RP2040 pins: no more than 0.5 V above the 3.3 V supply (RP2040 datasheet). RP2350 takes 5 V on GPIO only while its 3.3 V supply is on (RP2350 5 V). Safest to treat both as 3.3 V | Native USB | Kits |
| Blue Pill (STM32F103C8) | 3.3 V (2 to 3.6 V). Pins marked FT take 5 V with their internal pull-ups off; the rest, including PA0 to PA7, PB0, PB1 and PC0 to PC5, 4.0 V max (STM32F103 datasheet) | Its USB can't upload until you add a bootloader (stm32duino uploads): use ST-Link or serial | The Ender-3 V2 main board is an STM32F103 (Klipper Ender-3 V2) |
| SAMD21, SAMD51 (Adafruit M0, M4; Arduino Zero, MKR) | 3.3 V (Adafruit Feather M0, Adafruit Feather M4) | Native USB. Adafruit boards: UF2 bootloader (Adafruit Feather M4). Arduino Zero and MKR: SAM-BA bootloader, a port not a drive (Arduino SAMD bootloader) | Kits |
| ATtiny85, Digispark | 2.7 to 5.5 V; ATtiny85V 1.8 to 5.5 V (ATtiny85 datasheet) | Digispark: USB done in software (micronucleus) | Kits |

**5 V into a 3.3 V pin:** on some 3.3 V chips anything over 3.6 V does permanent damage (SparkFun logic). ESP32 input pins are rated 3.6 V absolute max (MicroPython ESP32). Bring 5 V signals down with a divider, such as SparkFun's 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ, or a level shifter (SparkFun logic); size others with the [Voltage divider](#ref/divider) calculator. An ATmega328P pin is rated 40 mA absolute max, 200 mA for the whole chip (ATmega328P datasheet): run relays and motors through a transistor.

**Drivers and ports:** CH340 usually installs itself. If not, get WCH's driver (file name CH341SER). It shows as USB-SERIAL CH340 (COMx) in Windows Device Manager, /dev/cu.wchusbserial… on a Mac, /dev/ttyUSB… on Linux (SparkFun CH340). CP2102: Silicon Labs driver (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting). No port at all: try another cable; power-bank cables often carry no data (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting). Close serial terminals before uploading (Cow Pi Nano). On Ubuntu, a CH340 that lsusb lists but that gives no /dev/ttyUSB0 may be blocked by the brltty package; removing it and rebooting fixed that for reporters (Ubuntu brltty CH340).

## Get into the bootloader

| Family | Normal upload | Force it or recover |
|---|---|---|
| Uno, Nano, Mega, Pro Mini | The USB-serial chip's DTR line resets the chip (SparkFun USB-serial) | Nano clones: Tools > Processor > **ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)**, which talks at 57,600 baud instead of 115,200 (Arduino boards.txt, Cow Pi Nano). Dead bootloader: burn one with a second Arduino as ISP (below) |
| Leonardo, Pro Micro (32U4) | The IDE opens the port at 1200 baud to reset it, then waits for the bootloader's port (Arduino boards.txt) | Short RST to GND **twice quickly**: the bootloader waits 8 s; pick its port and upload in that window. One reset gives under 750 ms (SparkFun Pro Micro) |
| ESP8266, ESP-01 | Adapter's DTR and RTS drive GPIO0 and EN (Espressif boot ESP8266) | GPIO0 to GND while it starts (Espressif boot ESP8266, Tasmota). Boot messages come at 74,880 baud (Espressif boot ESP8266) |
| ESP32 | DTR and RTS, as above (Espressif boot ESP32) | Hold **BOOT** (GPIO0), press and release **EN**, release BOOT (Espressif boot ESP32, MicroPython ESP32 tutorial). Or hold BOOT as the upload starts and let go when the IDE shows "Connecting…" (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting). Boot messages at 115,200 baud: DOWNLOAD_BOOT means download mode (Espressif boot ESP32) |
| ESP32-S2, S3, C3 on native USB | Straight over USB | Hold BOOT, press and release RESET (Arduino-ESP32 USB). BOOT is GPIO0 on the S3, GPIO9 on the C3 (Espressif boot S3, Espressif boot C3). After the first flash, reset by hand (Arduino-ESP32 USB) |
| Pico, Pico 2 | Copy a .uf2 file to its drive | Hold **BOOTSEL** while plugging in: drive RPI-RP2 (Pico) or RP2350 (Pico 2) appears. BOOTSEL is in ROM, so software can't brick it. To wipe the flash, copy nuke_universal.uf2 to it (Pico docs), or Adafruit's flash_nuke.uf2 on RP2040 (Adafruit CircuitPython troubleshooting), then reload firmware |
| SAMD21, SAMD51, nRF52 UF2 boards (not Arduino Zero or MKR: SAM-BA, port not drive) | Drive or IDE | Double-tap reset, about half a second apart: a …BOOT drive appears (FEATHERBOOT, FTHR840BOOT) and the LED goes green. Red: try another cable and port (Adafruit UF2, Adafruit nRF52840) |
| Blue Pill (STM32F103) | ST-Link on the 4-pin SWD header (stm32-base, stm32duino uploads). Never wire the ST-Link's 5 V pin (Greaseweazle ST-Link) | Serial: BOOT0 to 1 with BOOT1 left at 0 (ST community), reset, then cross the lines: adapter RX to PA9 (the chip's TX), adapter TX to PA10 (the chip's RX), 3.3 V adapter (STM32F103 datasheet). Set BOOT0 back to 0 and reset to run it |
| Black Pill (STM32F401, F411) | USB DFU | Hold BOOT0, press and release reset, then release BOOT0 0.5 s later. Still not seen: warm the chip to about 25 °C and retry (WeAct Black Pill) |
| ATtiny85, any AVR | ISP from a second Arduino running ArduinoISP: D10 to RESET, D11 MOSI, D12 MISO, D13 SCK; Programmer: Arduino as ISP (SparkFun bootloader) | Fuses, below |

**ESP-01 or bare ESP8266 module:** CH_PD (EN) and RST pulled up, GPIO15 pulled down, GPIO0 pulled up and taken to GND to flash. Use resistors, not direct wires (ESP8266 Arduino boards). It draws up to 70 mA, with peaks of 200 to 300 mA: a USB-serial adapter's or an Arduino's 3.3 V pin can't supply that (esptool ESP8266 troubleshooting). Use a separate 3.3 V supply, grounds joined.

**AVR fuses:** ISP needs the chip's clock. An ATtiny85 ships running at 1 MHz (8 MHz ÷ 8), and each half of the programmer's clock must last over 2 chip clocks, so use a slow programmer clock. If a fuse chose an external clock, feed a clock into its clock-in pin. If RSTDISBL is set (reset pin made into I/O), only high-voltage programming works: a dedicated HV programmer puts 11.5 to 12.5 V on RESET after 4.5 to 5.5 V is on VCC (ATtiny85 datasheet). Never put 12 V on a RESET line that is wired to an Arduino or adapter pin.

## Quirks that stop a board

| ESP32 pin | Problem |
|---|---|
| GPIO0 | Low at reset: download mode (Espressif boot ESP32) |
| GPIO2 | Must float or be low to enter download mode (Espressif boot ESP32); often the on-board LED (RNT ESP32 pinout) |
| GPIO12 | High at reset sets the flash to 1.8 V (Espressif boot ESP32): boot fails (RNT ESP32 pinout). A 1-Wire pull-up on GPIO12 does exactly this |
| GPIO15 | Low at reset silences boot messages (Espressif boot ESP32) |
| GPIO5 | Strapping pin (ESP-IDF GPIO) |
| GPIO6 to 11 | Wired to the flash chip: leave alone. GPIO16 and 17 are usually used by the module's flash or PSRAM too (ESP-IDF GPIO) |
| GPIO34 to 39 | Input only, no pull-ups (ESP-IDF GPIO) |
| ADC2 pins | Can't be read while Wi-Fi is on (ESP-IDF GPIO) |
| GPIO1, 3 | Serial for uploads and the REPL (MicroPython ESP32) |

- **ESP32-S3:** strapping GPIO0, 3, 45, 46; USB on GPIO19 and 20; GPIO26 to 32 are flash and PSRAM, and GPIO33 to 37 too on octal-PSRAM (R8) boards. **ESP32-C3:** strapping GPIO2, 8, 9 (download mode needs GPIO9 low and GPIO8 high); USB on GPIO18 and 19. Reusing USB pins as GPIO kills USB (ESP-IDF GPIO S3, ESP-IDF GPIO C3).
- **ESP8266:** at boot GPIO15 must be low and GPIO2 high or floating (Espressif boot ESP8266). The bare chip's analog input is 0 to 1.0 V (MicroPython ESP8266). NodeMCU 1.0 adds a 220k/100k divider (ESP8266 Arduino boards); the D1 mini takes 3.2 V max (WEMOS D1 mini).
- **Brownout resets** ("Brownout detector was triggered", or resets when Wi-Fi starts): ESP32 Wi-Fi transmit draws about 240 mA and the supply should give 0.5 A (ESP32 datasheet). Use a short data cable, another port or a powered hub (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting).
- **Uploads die halfway:** lower the baud rate (esptool troubleshooting). **Flashed but nothing runs:** some boards need flash mode dio (esptool ESP8266 troubleshooting).
- **Pico W, Pico 2 W:** the LED is on the wireless chip (WL_GPIO0), not GP25 (Pico docs). In MicroPython use Pin("LED") (MicroPython Pin).
- **32U4 sketches that break USB:** code that touches the USB set-up registers (PLLCSR) or was built for the wrong speed (3.3 V/8 MHz vs 5 V/16 MHz) gives "USB device not recognized". Double-tap reset and upload a good sketch (SparkFun Pro Micro).
- **ESP32-S2, S3, C3 on native USB:** the port vanishes if the sketch reuses the USB pins, and during deep sleep; to recover, GPIO0 (C3: GPIO9) low and reset (ESP-IDF USB console). No serial output: Tools > **USB CDC On Boot** > Enabled, upload again. A fast reboot loop can still hide messages (Arduino-ESP32 troubleshooting).
- **MicroPython stuck in main.py:** Ctrl-C at the REPL stops it, then `import os; os.remove('main.py')` (MicroPython boot). Reflashing alone usually won't help, as the files survive (MicroPython boot). Erase first, with the nuke file on a Pico or `esptool erase-flash` on an ESP (esptool commands), then reflash.
- **CircuitPython safe mode:** press reset once within 1 s of start-up (a slow double-click; a fast one opens the bootloader). Safe mode skips code.py and boot.py so you can fix them. At the REPL, `import storage` then `storage.erase_filesystem()` wipes the files. No REPL: copy flash_nuke.uf2 (RP2040) or erase_m0.uf2 (SAMD21 non-Express) to the BOOT drive (Adafruit CircuitPython troubleshooting).
- **CIRCUITPY drive corrupts:** without the Mu editor, Eject (Windows) or sync (Linux) before unplugging (Adafruit CircuitPython editing).

## Clones and knock-offs

| Board | Quirk | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Nano, Uno clones | CH340 USB chip. Nano clones often need the old bootloader setting (only the Nano menu has it; the Uno does not). Some carry an ATmega328PB, which reportedly gives "can't set com-state" errors (Cow Pi Nano) | CH340 driver; Processor: ATmega328P (Old Bootloader); for 328PB install its board support (Cow Pi Nano) |
| Pro Mini clones | No USB; 3.3 V and 5 V versions look alike (SparkFun Pro Mini) | Adapter at the board's voltage, its DTR to the GRN end (SparkFun USB-serial); pick the matching processor (SparkFun Pro Mini) |
| LGT8F328P "Nano" or "Pro Mini" (may be marked AVGA328P) | Not an ATmega328P: runs up to 32 MHz, has a DAC and more timers, no flash lock bits (lgt8fx) | Boards Manager URL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dbuezas/lgt8fx/master/package_lgt8fx_index.json, install "lgt8fx", choose the LGT8F328P board (lgt8fx) |
| LoLin "V3" NodeMCU | Not an official NodeMCU version; bigger than V2 boards; one reserve pin is USB power out, the other an extra GND (Frightanic NodeMCU) | Same as any ESP8266 board |
| ESP32 30-pin DevKit V1 clones | Auto-reset may fail. The 30-pin version leaves out GPIO6 to 11 (RNT ESP32 pinout) | Hold BOOT as the upload starts, let go at "Connecting…" (RNT ESP32 troubleshooting), or fit 10 µF from EN to GND (RNT failed to connect) |
| ESP32-CAM | No USB. Flash: GPIO0 to GND, press RST; remove the link and press RST to run (RNT ESP32-CAM). Brownouts | Power from its 5 V pin (never 5 V into 3V3), use a short data cable (RNT ESP32-CAM); keep TX and RX at 3.3 V (Tasmota). The ESP32-CAM-MB base adds a CH340C and buttons: if upload fails, hold IO0, tap RST, release IO0, upload (RNT ESP32-CAM-MB) |
| ESP32-C3 SuperMini, S3 clones | Native USB only; the port vanishes in deep sleep or if the sketch reuses the USB pins (ESP-IDF USB console) | Hold BOOT, tap RESET, release, upload; enable USB CDC On Boot (Arduino-ESP32 USB, Arduino-ESP32 troubleshooting) |
| Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V3 | ESP32-S3 with SX1262 radio; its CP2102 has no ESD protection; may not charge a battery over a USB-C to USB-C cable (Heltec docs, Meshtastic Heltec) | Fit the antenna before power-up: Meshtastic warns the radio can be damaged without one (Meshtastic Heltec, Meshtastic T-Beam) |
| LilyGO T-Beam | T-Beam Supreme and S3-Core: ESP32-S3, SX1262, GPS. Holder takes only unprotected flat-top 18650s (Meshtastic T-Beam) | Antenna first. To flash: hold BOOT, plug in, release after 2 to 3 s (Meshtastic T-Beam) |
| Digispark (ATtiny85) | Bootloader takes about 2 KB of the 8 KB flash; sketch starts about 5 s after power-up; P3 and P4 are the USB lines (Wolles Digispark) | Plug in only when the IDE asks (Wolles Digispark). Windows needs the libusb driver (micronucleus) |
| Blue Pill fakes: CS32, CKS32, GD32, APM32, "STM32FEB…" | Genuine STM32F103 answers ID 0x1ba01477; CS32 and CKS32 answer 0x2ba01477, so OpenOCD stops with "UNEXPECTED idcode". Some are marked as ST parts (Hackaday STM32 clones). Fakes may have two round dimples and smaller print (not proof alone: ST changed its markings in 2022), fail Blinky, or, on one tested board, would not program above 115,200 baud (CNX STM32 fakes). GD32: 108 MHz, flash in a separate chip, more sleep current, a short start-up delay (Hackaday STM32 clones). APM32: marked Geehy or APEX (CNX APM32) | OpenOCD: set CPUTAPID to 0 or the clone's ID (Hackaday STM32 clones). Test with Blinky first; ST's own tools may refuse clones (CNX STM32 fakes) |
| Blue Pill USB | D+ pull-up often 10 kΩ or 4.7 kΩ instead of 1.5 kΩ (stm32-base) | Replace it with 1.5 kΩ (stm32-base) |
| Waveshare RP2040-Zero | LED is a WS2812 RGB type, so plain blink code won't light it; Waveshare supplies a WS2812 demo. 2 MB flash, USB-C (Waveshare RP2040-Zero, Waveshare wiki) | Bootloader: press RESET, press BOOT, release RESET, then BOOT (Waveshare wiki) |
| YD-RP2040 (purple Pico clone) | USB-C, reset button, user button on GPIO24, RGB LED on GPIO23, 4, 8 or 16 MB flash (CircuitPython YD-RP2040) | Use firmware built for it where offered (CircuitPython YD-RP2040) |

## Reflashing ESP smart plugs and bulbs

- **DANGER: MAINS ELECTRICITY CAN KILL YOU. Unplug the device from the wall before you open it. Never have it plugged into mains while the case is open, or while a USB-serial adapter or computer is wired to it.** Mains reaching your serial wiring can electrocute you and will destroy the adapter and your computer. Power it only from the adapter's 3.3 V or a separate 3.3 V supply. Close the case fully before it goes back into a socket (Tasmota, ESPHome serial).
- **You need** a USB-serial adapter with data and power at 3.3 V. Some adapters switch data to 3.3 V but keep 5 V on the power pin, which destroys the chip (Tasmota). ESPHome suggests a CH340 adapter. Some adapters can't supply enough current: then use a separate 3.3 V supply (ESPHome serial).
- **Wire** 3.3 V, GND, adapter TX to chip RX, RX to TX; hold GPIO0 to GND while it powers up. Release it after a few seconds, or leave it grounded through the erase and write, but remove it before the first normal boot (Tasmota); a power cycle between erase and write may help (ESPHome serial). Failing? Swap TX and RX (ESPHome serial).
- **Back up** the maker's firmware: `esptool --port PORT read-flash 0 ALL backup.bin` (esptool commands). Then erase and write `tasmota.bin` at 0x0 with `-fm dout` (ESP8266) or `tasmota32.factory.bin` at 0x0 (ESP32). Join the tasmota_… Wi-Fi network and open http://192.168.4.1 within 3 minutes (Tasmota). Tasmota's and MicroPython's guides use the older spellings `esptool.py`, `erase_flash`, `write_flash` (Tasmota, MicroPython ESP32 download).
- **Not ESP inside?** Beken BK72xx, Realtek RTL8710 and LN882H chips are common in Tuya devices. ESPHome's LibreTiny platform runs on them, with its own UART flashing guides; tuya-cloudcutter can flash some BK72xx over the air (ESPHome LibreTiny). Tuya-Convert now fails on almost all devices (Tasmota).

## Programming with no internet: download now

| Get | Notes |
|---|---|
| Arduino IDE 1.x zip, set up portable | A folder named portable inside keeps sketches, libraries and cores together; copy it to a USB stick. Windows and Linux only (Arduino portable) |
| Board packages and libraries | Boards Manager downloads them, so install now: e.g. ESP32 from https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json (Arduino-ESP32 install) and ESP8266 from https://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json (ESP8266 Arduino install). Add lgt8fx, OneWire and DallasTemperature too |
| Thonny | Python built in on Windows and Mac (Thonny); Raspberry Pi's Pico MicroPython guide covers it (Pico MicroPython) |
| MicroPython firmware | .uf2 for Pico boards (Pico MicroPython); .bin for ESP32, written at 0x1000, and for C3 and S3, written at 0 (MicroPython ESP32 download, MicroPython C3 download, MicroPython S3 download) |
| CircuitPython .uf2 files and the library bundle | Bundle must match CircuitPython's major version (CircuitPython libraries). The board shows up as a CIRCUITPY drive (Adafruit CircuitPython install): edit code.py, no compiler or uploader (Adafruit CircuitPython) |
| esptool | `pip install esptool` needs Python 3.10 or newer, or take the standalone builds from its GitHub releases (esptool install) |
| Tasmota | tasmota.bin from http://ota.tasmota.com/tasmota/release/ and tasmota32.factory.bin from https://ota.tasmota.com/tasmota32/release/ (Tasmota) |
| Rescue files and drivers | nuke_universal.uf2, flash_nuke.uf2, erase_m0.uf2; CH340 and CP210x drivers |

**Offline help in the NOMAD libraries:** Arduino Q&A, Raspberry Pi Q&A, Electronics Q&A, Robotics Q&A, and the DevDocs C++ Docs and Python Docs.
